meta.descriptionEn: On 4 November 1922, a workman in the Valley of the Kings uncovered a single step cut into the rock. Within weeks, Howard Carter was peering through a tiny hole by candlelight, and what he saw changed archaeology forever. This documentary follows the search for Tutankhamun's lost tomb: the years of failure, a patron on the edge of giving up, the tense moments at the sealed door, and the thousands of treasures inside. Who was the boy king whose tomb was hidden under workers' huts? How did it survive robbers? And why did newspapers claim a curse followed those who entered? We separate documented fact from legend and ask what the discovery still leaves unanswered.
meta.descriptionUr: 4 November 1922 ko Valley of the Kings mein ek mazdoor ko pathar mein tarashi hui ek seerhi mili. Chand hafton baad Howard Carter moam batti ki roshni mein ek chhote se surakh se andar jhaank raha tha. Is documentary mein hum Tutankhamun ke gum shuda maqbare ki talash, Lord Carnarvon ka sabr, hazaron khazano ki kahani, aur fir'aunon ki bad-dua ki afwahon ka sach dekhenge. Kya waqai koi curse tha? articleEn: It is 26 November 1922 in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. At the bottom of a staircase stands a sealed door, and in front of it stands Howard Carter. With a chisel, he makes a small hole in the upper left corner of the door. Then he brings a lit candle close to the opening. Lord Carnarvon, standing beside him, asks, "Can you see anything?" Carter answers, "Yes, wonderful things!" The line is still famous today, although in his journal entry for the same day he wrote, "Yes, it is wonderful."

So what lay behind this door? Whose tomb did the staircase lead to, and how did such an ancient place survive? Who owned the tomb, and why was a man with so much wealth buried in such a small one? Then there is the notorious story: that anyone who set foot inside suffered a curse. Was there any truth in it?

This article begins with Tutankhamun's short life, then follows the story of Howard Carter, and finally looks at the truth about the curse. Let's go behind that small hole. The discovery gave the whole world a new interest in ancient Egypt.

articleEn: Let's step back. Tutankhamun was born during the reign of Akhenaten, in the Amarna Period, the final phase of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty. His original name was Tutankhaten, meaning "living image of Aten." The name reflected the religious shift known as Atenism. Who his parents were is still debated, because no surviving inscription clearly says. DNA testing identified his father as the mummy from tomb KV55. That mummy is thought to be either Akhenaten or Smenkhkare. His mother is known as The Younger Lady. Genetic research suggests his parents may have been brother and sister, though some experts question that conclusion.

At about 8 or 9 years old he became pharaoh. After Akhenaten, the brief reigns of Smenkhkare and Neferneferuaten had already passed. On taking the throne he adopted the name Nebkheperure. His reign lasted about nine years and is usually dated to c. 1332 to 1323 BC. One clarification is needed: depending on the chronology used, these dates can shift by roughly ten to twenty years.

His most notable achievement was the restoration of traditional religion. In his third regnal year he ended the supremacy of Aten and placed the god Amun at the top again. In this period the king took the name Tutankhamun, and the queen's name became Ankhesenamun. The royal court left Amarna and moved to Memphis. The old rights of Amun's priests were restored, and repairs on the temples began. Some experts think advisers made these decisions because the king was so young.

The record of these works survives on the Restoration Stela, found at Karnak in July 1905, seventeen years before the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb. His treasurer, Maya, played an important part in the programme. Under a decree of the eighth year, the king had temple offerings restored. In his private life he married Ankhesenpaaten, who later became Ankhesenamun. Their two daughters died at birth or soon after.

The last certain date is Year 9, which is why most experts consider his reign to be about nine years long. He was about 19 when he died. Ay and then Horemheb followed him, and with his death the royal line of the Eighteenth Dynasty came to an end. Was his death sudden? And where was he buried? The next section answers these questions.

articleEn: No record of Tutankhamun's death survives, so we have to rely on scientific research and archaeology. According to Zahi Hawass's team, his death resulted from several factors, including a leg injury, perhaps from a fall, and severe malaria. Another theory held that a 1968 X-ray showed two pieces of bone inside the skull, suggesting he might have been murdered. Later X-rays and CT scan analysis proved this theory wrong. The fragments were loose and were the result of modern methods used when the mummy was unwrapped.

Another idea was that he died in a chariot accident. It was based on a missing part of the chest. But in Carter's photographs taken in 1926, that part is intact. The damage was probably caused later by thieves who stole a beaded collar.

Now to the burial. Tutankhamun may have started building a royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings, but it was unfinished when he died. So he was buried in a small non-royal tomb, which was adapted for the purpose. It may have been made for someone else. This arrangement made it possible to keep to a 70-day gap between death and burial. Plant remains indicate that the burial took place between late February and April.

At the funeral, Ay performed the opening of the mouth ritual, which was normally the next pharaoh's duty. So Ay's standing was clear. Horemheb, the commander-in-chief of the army, later became pharaoh after Ay. Experts disagree about whether he was present at the funeral. Horemheb led a major campaign to erase the names of the Amarna-period kings. He damaged Ay's tomb, but probably left Tutankhamun's alone out of respect.

The tomb was probably robbed at least twice within a few months of being sealed. Among the missing items were perishable oils and perfumes. After these events there are signs that the tomb was repaired. Then, slowly, its location was forgotten. Rubble from the digging of KV9, more than 150 years later, piled up over its entrance. Workers' houses were also built above. That same rubble and those huts became the tomb's protection. The question is who would go looking for it centuries later.

articleEn: So who was the man who found the tomb? His name was Howard Carter, and his story begins in a small town. Carter was born on 9 May 1874 in Kensington, London. He was the youngest of eleven children. His mother was Martha Joyce. His father, Samuel John Carter, was an artist and illustrator who helped develop his son's artistic talent.

Carter was often ill as a child. Three of his siblings had died young, so he was sent to Swaffham, where a nurse looked after him. Swaffham was also his parents' ancestral town. There he received only a limited formal education, but he had clear talent for drawing. Nearby stood Didlington Hall, the home of the Amherst family, which held a large collection of Egyptian antiques. This is where Carter's interest in Egypt began. Lady Amherst was impressed by his art.

In 1891, at her suggestion, the Egypt Exploration Fund sent Carter to assist Percy Newberry. The job was to excavate and record the Middle Kingdom tombs at Beni Hasan. Carter was only 17, yet he improved the methods of copying tomb pictures. In 1892 he spent a season at Amarna under Flinders Petrie. This was the capital founded by the pharaoh Akhenaten. Then from 1894 to 1899 he worked with Édouard Naville at Deir el-Bahari, where he recorded the wall reliefs of Hatshepsut's temple.

In 1899, on Gaston Maspero's personal recommendation, Carter was made Inspector of Monuments for Upper Egypt, based in Luxor. There he oversaw many excavations and restorations in Thebes. Theodore Davis's systematic exploration of the Valley of the Kings also took place under his supervision. In 1904, after disputes with local people over tomb thefts, he was moved to the Inspectorate of Lower Egypt. Even so, he was praised for improving site protection.

Then came the Saqqara Affair. On 8 January 1905 there was a clash between site guards and French tourists. Carter supported the Egyptian staff and refused to apologise. After a formal inquiry, Carter resigned from the Antiquities Service in 1905. For almost three years he lived in Luxor without a regular job. How did he get by? He painted watercolours and sold them to tourists, and in 1906 he also worked as a freelance draughtsman for Theodore Davis.
Up to this point, Carter looked like an unemployed painter. But the next year a man was about to enter his life who would change everything.

articleEn: Carter's fortunes changed in 1907. Gaston Maspero recommended him to Lord Carnarvon, because Maspero knew Carter would use modern archaeological methods and recording. Carnarvon's full name was George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon. His health had been weak since a car accident in 1901. His doctor advised a warm climate, so Carnarvon came to Egypt in 1903. It was here that he developed an interest in Egyptology.

Carter began supervising excavations of nobles' tombs at Deir el-Bahari for him. Soon the two had a good working relationship. According to Lady Burghclere, Carnarvon's sister, they worked together for the next sixteen years, and mutual respect and affection, along with a shared goal, held them together.

At that time the concession for the Valley of the Kings belonged to Theodore Davis, who held it from 1905 to 1914. In that period Davis found ten tombs, including the nearly intact but non-royal tomb of Yuya and Thuya, the parents of Queen Tiye. In later years, however, nothing major turned up. In KV58 Davis found a few items bearing Tutankhamun's name, along with an embalming cache, KV54. Davis believed this was the king's lost tomb. In his findings he wrote, "I fear the Valley of the Tombs is exhausted." In other words, Davis thought nothing was left in the Valley. But was that true? History would prove it wrong.

Carter and Carnarvon hoped to get the concession when Davis gave it up. For the time being they had to work in other parts of the Theban Necropolis. The wait lasted seven years. Then in 1914 Lord Carnarvon received the concession to excavate in the Valley of the Kings. Carter already had experience of the Valley, having supervised Davis's exploration as Inspector. He took charge of the work. The plan was a systematic search for tombs that earlier expeditions had missed, especially Tutankhamun's.

But the First World War stopped everything. During the war years Carter worked for the British Government as a diplomatic courier and translator. At the end of 1917 he resumed the excavation with full energy. One source dates the start of the search to 1915 and another to 1914. Despite years of effort, little of note was turning up. And Carnarvon's patience would reach its limit in 1922.

articleEn: By 1922 Lord Carnarvon was not satisfied with the results. Years of digging had produced very little, so he considered withdrawing his funding. Imagine if the effort had ended there; history might have been very different. But after talking with Carter, Carnarvon agreed to fund one last season. That meant just one more season in the Valley of the Kings, and the fate of the whole campaign would be decided by its result.

Carter returned to the Valley of the Kings and began examining a row of huts he had left a few seasons earlier. These were the huts of ancient workmen. Beneath them lay a heap of rock debris, and the spot was very close to KV9. Because of this closeness, the area remained unexcavated until 1922. Digging there could block the route of tourists going to KV9. Remember, this was the same place where, more than 150 years after the burial, the debris from KV9 had covered the entrance to Tutankhamun's tomb.

Carter began digging in early November 1922, before the peak of the tourist season. The crew cleared the huts and the rock debris below. Then came 4 November 1922. That day a worker discovered the first step of a staircase cut into the rock. According to Carter's own account, the workmen found the step while digging beneath the remains of the huts. But there is another version of the story. Other accounts say the discovery was made by a boy named Hussein Abdul Rasoul, a water boy who was digging outside his assigned work area. Sources record both versions, so it is hard to say what the truth was. What they have in common is that a step was seen first.

Carter partially excavated the staircase, enough to expose the upper surface of a doorway. The door was covered with mud plaster. It bore oval seal impressions with cartouches, which are hieroglyphic nameplates. But the marks were indistinct, so they did not give a clear answer. Here Carter made an important decision. He had the staircase filled in again, and sent a telegram to inform Carnarvon, who was in England.

Carnarvon arrived in Egypt about two and a half weeks later, on 23 November, accompanied by his daughter, Lady Evelyn Herbert. Now everyone's eyes were on the refilled staircase. What was below? A tomb, or only an old cache? The next few days would answer that question.

articleEn: On 24 November 1922 the whole staircase was cleared. On the outer door a seal was found bearing Tutankhamun's cartouche. When this door was removed, a corridor filled with rubble lay behind it. It was cleared, and at last the door of the tomb itself came into view. On 26 November, Carter, Carnarvon, Lady Evelyn and the assistant Arthur Callender were there. Carter made a small hole in the upper left corner of the door, using a chisel that his grandmother had given him for his 17th birthday.

Then he looked inside by candlelight. He saw many treasures of gold and ebony in place. He did not yet know whether it was a tomb or just an old cache. But between two sentinel statues, a sealed door could be clearly seen. This was the moment when Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything. Carter replied, "Yes, wonderful things!" although in his journal that day he had written, "Yes, it is wonderful."

The tomb was then secured so that it could be entered the next day in the presence of an official of the Egyptian Department of Antiquities. But it is alleged that the same night these four entered the tomb without permission. If so, they were the first people to enter in modern times. According to some sources they even went as far as the inner burial chamber. In this account, a small hole in the sealed door is mentioned, through which the three people squeezed.

The next morning, 27 November, the tomb was formally inspected in the presence of an Egyptian official. Callender installed electric lighting there. When the lights came on, a huge collection of gold-decorated couches, chests, thrones and other items came into view. Then came another important day. On 17 February 1923, just after two in the afternoon, the seal was broken in front of about twenty selected witnesses. They included Lord Carnarvon, several Egyptian officials, museum representatives and staff of the Government Press Bureau. By February 1923 the antechamber was empty except for the two sentinel statues. All eyes were now on that closed door.

Now a controversial point. According to letters published in 2022, Carter kept some items for himself before the tomb was officially opened. About a whm amulet, Rex Engelbach wrote to Alan Gardiner that it had certainly been stolen from Tutankhamun's tomb. So as soon as it opened, the tomb revealed both treasures and controversy. And soon another story was about to begin: the story of the curse.

articleEn: Once the tomb was opened, news of it began to appear in newspapers around the world. Then a rumour spread that is still alive today: the curse of the pharaohs. Carnarvon was the patron who had funded Carter's last season. On 17 February 1923 he was also among the witnesses when the tomb was opened. It is said that the rumours may also have been fuelled by the wish to raise newspaper sales. The emphasis was on the fact that some people who had visited the tomb died soon after.

The most famous name was Lord Carnarvon. He died on 5 April 1923, five months after the first step of the tomb was found. This closeness added fuel to the rumours. But what was the real medical cause? He died of pneumonia that developed after facial erysipelas. Erysipelas is a streptococcal infection that affects the skin and the tissue beneath it. It was an ordinary illness, not the work of some mysterious force.

In addition, Carnarvon had been in a car accident in 1901, after which he was quite frail. His doctor advised a warm climate, so the Carnarvon family went to Egypt in 1903, where he became interested in Egyptology. Along with the pressure of the excavation, he was already in a weakened state when the infection progressed to pneumonia. So the cause of his death was medical.

Now look at the numbers. According to one study, 58 people were present when the tomb and sarcophagus were opened, and only 8 of them died within twelve years. That means 50 of the 58 were still alive after twelve years. This does not fit the claim of a curse. Howard Carter himself died in 1939 of lymphoma. He was 64, about 17 years after the discovery.

Lady Evelyn Herbert, Carnarvon's daughter and one of the early people to enter the tomb, lived another 57 years. She died in 1980. The American archaeologist J.O. Kinnaman was also among the last survivors. He died in 1961, 39 years after the event. So what is the conclusion? Illness, frail health and coincidence of timing together became a famous story.

Friends, we find no solid basis for the curse in the sources. But the real treasure of the tomb was something else. What was found inside, and how did it change the world? We look at that in the final section.

articleEn: What was finally found in the tomb? Tutankhamun's tomb is the only royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings found in a nearly intact condition. In all, 5,398 items were found there. They included a solid gold coffin, a face mask, thrones, archery bows, trumpets, furniture, food, wine and sandals. It took Carter 10 years to catalogue everything. Think of it: a whole decade passed in understanding and cataloguing a single tomb.

A dagger was also found, whose iron blade, according to analysis from the 1960s, appears to be made from a meteorite. Many burial goods were originally made for someone else. On a golden Nut pectoral, Marc Gabolde showed traces of the original cartouches of Neferneferuaten.

Now to the world beyond the tomb. In 1962 an exhibition of Tutankhamun was held at the Louvre Museum, which about 1.2 million visitors saw. Then from 1972 to 1979 the tour The Treasures of Tutankhamun ran. It began on 30 March 1972 at the British Museum in London, where more than 1.6 million people came. In the United States the Metropolitan Museum of Art organised the exhibition. More than 8 million people saw it there.

Right after the discovery, in the 1920s, 'King Tut' became a popular name. The 1923 song 'Old King Tut' became famous, and products and businesses named 'King Tut' appeared. In 1978 Steve Martin's novelty song 'King Tut' came out, selling more than a million copies as a single. In 2007, exactly 85 years after Carter's discovery, Tutankhamun's mummy was put on display in the tomb in a climate-controlled glass box. In 2009 the tomb was closed for restoration. The five-year plan was set back by the 2011 Egyptian revolution, and the tomb reopened in February 2019. According to sources, the collection was moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2025. Before that, some of it had travelled around the world.

Many questions remain today. Who were Tutankhamun's parents? DNA testing points to the KV55 mummy and The Younger Lady. But the identification of KV55 is disputed. Some experts consider it Akhenaten and some Smenkhkare. For this reason, questions are also raised about the reliability of the genetic data. As for his death, Hawass's team believes that a leg fracture and severe malaria together caused it. But no written record exists.

So, friends, a small hole, a candle and a question changed the world. What do you think is the tomb's biggest secret? If you liked this story, like the video, subscribe to the channel, and be sure to share your opinion in the comments. Thank you!

shorts.text: کیا واقعی Tutankhamun کے tomb پر کوئی curse تھا؟ Tomb کھلتے ہی دنیا بھر کے اخباروں میں خبریں چھپنے لگیں، اور پھر curse of the pharaohs کی افواہ پھیل گئی۔ سب سے مشہور نام Lord Carnarvon کا تھا۔ ان کا انتقال 5 April 1923 کو ہوا، یعنی tomb کی پہلی سیڑھی ملنے کے پانچ مہینے بعد۔ لوگوں نے اسے curse کہہ دیا۔ مگر طبی وجہ pneumonia تھی، جو چہرے کے skin infection کے بعد ہوا۔ 1901 کے ایک car accident کے بعد سے ان کی صحت کمزور تھی۔ ایک study کے مطابق tomb اور sarcophagus کھلتے وقت موجود 58 لوگوں میں سے صرف 8 بارہ سال کے اندر فوت ہوئے۔ Howard Carter 1939 میں 64 سال کی عمر میں فوت ہوئے، اور Lady Evelyn 1980 تک زندہ رہیں۔ تو یہ افواہ اتنی مشہور کیوں ہو گئی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya waqai Tutankhamun ke tomb par koi curse tha? Tomb khulte hi duniya bhar ke akhbaaron mein khabren chhapne lagin, aur phir curse of the pharaohs ki afwaah phail gayi. Sab se mashhoor naam Lord Carnarvon ka tha. Un ka intiqal 5 April 1923 ko hua, yani tomb ki pehli seerhi milne ke paanch mahine baad. Logon ne ise curse keh diya. Magar tibbi wajah pneumonia thi, jo chehre ke skin infection ke baad hua. 1901 ke aik car accident ke baad se un ki sehat kamzor thi. Aik study ke mutabiq tomb aur sarcophagus khulte waqt mojood 58 logon mein se sirf 8 barah saal ke andar faut hue. Howard Carter 1939 mein 64 saal ki umr mein faut hue, aur Lady Evelyn 1980 tak zinda rahin. To yeh afwaah itni mashhoor kyun ho gayi? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: Lord Carnarvon died five months after the tomb's first step was found, and the curse rumour began. Here is what the records actually show.
